cards.title: The optimal polynomial-time approximation of EFX
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine α_alg = sup{α∈[0,1] : there is a deterministic algorithm that, on every finite instance of nonnegative rational additive goods, returns a complete α-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the binary input length}. The number of agents is unbounded and part of the input.
cards.why: Separates the efficiently attainable fairness guarantee from the purely existential EFX frontier.

progress.text: A polynomial algorithm achieves the universal factor (√5−1)/2.
The survey retains the gap beyond this general EFX approximation and distinguishes exact existence from computation.
A preprint improves the 2/3-EFX guarantee to eight agents, while retaining about 0.618 as the known general frontier.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 goods and an explicit table of values v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g, with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. An allocation (A₁,…,A_n) partitions [m] into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is α-EFX if v_i(A_i)≥α·v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every pair i,j and every g∈A_j, including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty A_j imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed α in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most C(N+1)^k on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on α, but not on n, m or the valuations. α is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since α=0 is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a real a∈[0,1] and prove that a=α_alg: achievable polynomial-time factors approach a arbitrarily closely from below, and no such algorithm guarantees any factor greater than a within [0,1]. An algorithm attaining a suffices for the first part but is not required. A conditional hardness result establishes only the corresponding conditional bound; a guarantee for one fixed number of agents does not establish the universal value.

context_blocks.title: How to read the approximation factor
context_blocks.text: Higher α means a stronger guarantee, with α=1 giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when α≤4/5. This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

context_blocks.title: The known general guarantee
context_blocks.text: Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor (√5−1)/2≈0.618. Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are (√5−1)/2≤α_alg≤1; the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

context_blocks.title: Why the number of agents matters
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint reports a 2/3-EFX algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Existence, computation and a supremum
context_blocks.text: TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even α_alg=1 would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.

sentences: All indivisible goods must be allocated among agents with nonnegative additive values.
An α-EFX allocation lets each agent retain at least an α fraction of the value she assigns to any other bundle after any one good is removed.
The question asks for the supremum factor guaranteed by deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for arbitrarily many agents.
A general factor of about 0.618 is known, while recent 2/3 guarantees cover only bounded numbers of agents.
The computational supremum differs from an existence guarantee and need not be attained by one algorithm.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
